channel.title: EEB Daily
channel.description: Nightly one-page evolutionary biology newsletter from the Blackmon lab, Texas A&M.

item.title: No. 40: Common mutations can beat fitter alternatives
item.description: New mathematical approximations explain when the supply of mutations outweighs their relative fitness advantages.

item.title: No. 39: Host movement changes the evolution of parasite harm
item.description: A theoretical study shows why accounting for host behavior changes predictions about the evolution of virulence.

item.title: No. 38: A better rattlesnake genome restores missing venom genes
item.description: A chromosome-scale reference recovers venom loci obscured by an earlier, fragmented genome assembly.

item.title: No. 37: Cheap genotypes still reveal inbreeding
item.description: Sparse genetic data can recover overall inbreeding even when the age of shared ancestry remains difficult to resolve.

item.title: No. 36: Immunization can help frogs survive chytrid
item.description: A synthesis of 36 studies finds that some experimental immunization approaches reduce fungal infections or deaths in amphibians.

item.title: No. 35: Gene interactions hide evolutionary distance
item.description: A continuous-time protein model shows how epistasis can slow sequence evolution without changing average rates at individual sites.

item.title: No. 34: The gut harbors missing relatives of poxviruses
item.description: A worldwide metagenomic survey reveals large DNA viruses whose evolutionary history points to single-celled gut inhabitants.

item.title: No. 33: Cell family trees can tell time without one universal clock
item.description: A new Bayesian method dates immune-cell ancestry while allowing mutation rates to change with cell state.

item.title: No. 32: Pig Y chromosomes reveal moving centromeres
item.description: Complete pig genomes reveal that even the chromosome's cell-division attachment site can shift across lineages.

item.title: No. 31: Small mitochondrial differences can have big effects
item.description: Fly crosses reveal that interactions among mitochondrial genomes, nuclear genomes and environmental stress can matter more than evolutionary distance alone.

item.title: No. 30: Losing a firefly's glow rewires more than one gene
item.description: Genomes and gene knockdowns reveal how disappearing adult light organs coincide with lost gene families, changed regulation and altered cuticle development.

item.title: No. 29: Ant chromosomes shuffle at extreme speed
item.description: A new map of California harvester ant chromosomes links exceptionally frequent crossovers to genome diversity and GC-rich DNA, without clear evidence of stronger protein-level selection.

item.title: No. 28: Algal chromosomes persist inside mammalian cells
item.description: A laboratory fusion experiment shows that host epigenetic regulation can help foreign eukaryotic DNA survive for many generations.

item.title: No. 27: Male and female lizards change size at different speeds
item.description: Separating male and female traits reveals evolutionary patterns that a single measure of sexual dimorphism misses.

item.title: No. 26: A bottleneck does not guarantee genetic recovery
item.description: New theory separates the loss of inbreeding depression from the harder recovery of population fitness.

item.title: No. 25: Most protist branches are still missing from our maps
item.description: A global search of environmental DNA exposes large gaps in the reference tree of microbial eukaryotes.

item.title: No. 24: Sex chromosomes have no single regulatory solution
item.description: A new synthesis finds that the rules of dosage compensation and germline silencing vary widely across animals.

item.title: No. 23: The chordate body plan has deeper roots
item.description: Experiments in a sea anemone suggest that embryonic organizer logic predates the origin of bilaterian animals.

item.title: No. 22: A fungal isolate carries genomes from two species
item.description: Reanalysis of two clinical fungal genomes reveals an interspecies hybrid and an unsampled parental lineage.

item.title: No. 21: Scale insects lost their X twice
item.description: New insect genomes reveal two distinct ways an ancestral X chromosome can lose its role in determining sex.

item.title: No. 20: Food smells switch on a fly's mating drive
item.description: A fruit specialist ties courtship to food odor and social motion through neural circuits that also exist in less dependent relatives.

item.title: No. 19: Bat DNA reveals a hidden conservation crisis
item.description: Mitochondrial sequences uncover 95 candidate lineages, but their identity and projected extinction risk need more precise tests.

item.title: No. 18: Jumping DNA can swell a genome, then shrink it
item.description: A new simulator reconstructs how mobile DNA can expand and contract genomes, suggesting that preventing transposon invasions may matter more than cleanup afterward.

item.title: No. 17: A selfish centromere builds an oversized chromosome
item.description: Monkeyflower genome assemblies reveal how a driving chromosome gathered rearrangements, repeated DNA and extra genes without yet revealing which change makes it cheat.

item.title: No. 16: Deleting one gene reverses frog sex
item.description: A newly evolved W-linked copy of wnt3 is required for female development in African clawed frogs, and its knockout produces fertile males.

item.title: No. 15: Microbial immune memories turn over across ecosystems
item.description: A census of nearly 800 million CRISPR spacers finds rapid turnover and warns that a viral match does not always identify a true host.

item.title: No. 14: Water gives body size more room to shift
item.description: Across more than 21,000 vertebrates, inferred changes in favored body size were larger and more frequent in aquatic lineages than on land or in the air.

item.title: No. 13: Close archaeal relatives of eukaryotes lack organelles
item.description: Two newly cultured relatives of eukaryotes challenge the idea that their archaeal ancestor already had complex internal membranes.

item.title: No. 12: Egg mimicry speeds the decay of a sex chromosome
item.description: In cuckoo finches, selection on maternally inherited egg colours is linked to W chromosome gene loss and rapid mitochondrial evolution.

item.title: No. 11: Fern sugar conduits narrowed through deep time
item.description: Living and fossil fern tissues reveal an evolutionary shift toward narrower sugar-transport cells, with consequences for flow still awaiting direct tests.
